To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the conical-cylindrically shaped nanopores are the best model for nanopore geometry determination and that the conductance-based nanopore geometry determination method is limited by a large number of free parameters.

the conductance of a solid-state nanopore with an exponential-cylinrical radial profile is not uniquely geometry-optimized; several simplified models generate quantitative agreement with the experimental conductance, but errors in key geometrical parameters can exceed 40%; and a tractable conical cylindrical model affords a good characterization of nanopore size/shape, with errors of <1% for the radius.

the conductance of a nanopore with an exponential radial profile is not uniquely determined by the geometry of the nanopore and that a conical-cylindrically shaped nanopore provides a good approximation to the conductance of the exponential nanopore.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding and improving the ability to characterize nanopore geometry from conductance data.
the determination of solid-state nanopore geometry from the conductance of the nanopore in an electrolyte solution.
understanding the performance limits of conductance-based determination of the geometry of solid-state nanopores.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
conductance is not a reliable method to characterize the shape and size of a solid-state nanopore.
the conductance of a surface-charged solid-state nanopore is not sufficient to uniquely determine its geometry.
the conductance of a nanopore with an exponential-cylinder profile cannot be used as a reliable method of characterizing its geometry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the conical-cylindrically-shaped model is the most accurate for the conductance, and the cylindrical-exponential model is the most robust for the geometry.
a conical-cylindrically shaped solid-state nanopore is a good approximation for a nanopore that can be characterized by its conductance.

, for a nanopore with an exponential-cylinder geometry, the conductance is a function of three geometric parameters: the radius of the cylindrical core, the radius of the exponential-cylinder shell, and the thickness of the shell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the conductance of solid-state nanopores can be used to determine the nanopore geometry, but only if the geometry is constrained to be cylindrical and if the pore size and geometry are small enough.
the conductance is a powerful tool for characterizing nanopores but is subject to a number of constraints that must be considered in the interpretation of experimental data.
the electrolyte-dependent nanopore conductance alone is insufficient for uniquely identifying the nanopore geometry.
